settings.heading: A local practice that gets to know you
settings.body:
We’re a family-owned practice on Stokes Street, close to Piccones IGA and the shops and health services of Edmonton.

We believe continuity matters. Seeing the same dentist from one visit to the next means your dentist knows your history, remembers what worries you, and notices changes early.

Whether you need a routine check-up, a filling, a new tooth or help in an emergency, our aim is the same: clear explanations, honest advice and care that goes at your pace.

settings.heading: Dental care for the whole family
settings.intro: From six-monthly check-ups to replacing missing teeth, our dentists provide general, preventive, restorative and cosmetic treatment at one practice. Choose a treatment to read what it involves, what to consider and what to expect.

items.title: Check-ups and cleans
items.text: An examination of your teeth, gums and jaw, X-rays where needed, then a scale, clean and polish. You leave with a printed plan if anything needs attention.

items.title: Children’s dentistry
items.text: Relaxed, positive visits that help children feel at home at the dentist, with problems found early. Free dentistry for eligible children.

items.title: Fillings
items.text: Early decay is removed and the tooth restored with white, tooth-coloured filling material, usually in a single visit.

items.title: Mouthguards
items.text: Custom-fitted mouthguards made from impressions of your teeth, for a snug, comfortable fit during contact sport.

items.title: Crowns and bridges
items.text: A crown reinforces a cracked or heavily filled tooth. A bridge fills a gap using the teeth on either side.

items.title: Root canal therapy
items.text: When a tooth's nerve is badly inflamed or has died, root canal treatment can often save the tooth instead of removing it.

items.title: Extractions
items.text: When a tooth can't be saved, we explain why, talk through your worries and take it slowly so you stay comfortable.

items.title: Wisdom teeth
items.text: A consultation and X-ray show whether your wisdom teeth are a problem. Removal is only recommended when it's needed.

items.title: Dental implants
items.text: A titanium post replaces the root of a missing tooth and supports a natural-looking crown fixed in place.

items.title: Dentures
items.text: First dentures, replacements for loose ones, or implant-retained dentures, planned around comfort and fit.

items.title: Teeth whitening
items.text: Professional whitening supervised by your dentist, starting with a check so you know what result to expect.

items.title: Cosmetic veneers
items.text: Thin porcelain shells bonded to the front of teeth to improve gaps, stains, chips and worn or short edges.

items.title: Invisalign
items.text: Clear, removable aligners that gradually straighten teeth, without brackets or wires. Suitability is assessed first.

items.title: Emergency dental care
items.text: Toothache, a broken tooth, swelling or lost dentures. We set aside appointments every day for urgent problems.

Alex wanted to be a dentist from early childhood. He grew up in Victoria, earned his dental degree from La Trobe University and completed his Masters in rural Victoria before moving to Queensland.

He has worked across Queensland, from Brisbane to Townsville, and is now proud to call Cairns home.

Alex enjoys all aspects of general dentistry and puts a high value on continuing education, regularly attending courses run by leaders in the field. His training has taken him overseas to learn techniques in dental implants and wisdom teeth surgery.

Outside dentistry, Alex loves time on the water fishing and with friends.

items.question: How should I look after my teeth between visits?
items.answer: brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, clean between your teeth every day, spit out the toothpaste rather than rinsing, and limit sugary food and drinks. Sources: Australian Dental Association, healthdirect.

items.question: Why do my gums bleed when I brush?
items.answer: bleeding gums can be an early sign of gum disease, though there can be other causes. Keep brushing gently, and book a check-up so your dentist can find the cause. Source: healthdirect.

items.question: What does a scale and clean do?
items.answer: It removes plaque and hardened tartar that brushing and flossing can’t shift, from your teeth and around your gums, then polishes the teeth smooth. Check-ups and cleans

items.question: When should my child first see a dentist?
items.answer: Australian advice is to book a first visit when the first teeth come through, or by around 12 months of age. Fun, positive early visits help children feel comfortable at the dentist. Source: Australian Dental Association.

items.question: Which toothpaste should my child use?
items.answer: from the first tooth to 18 months, clean teeth with a soft brush and water unless your dental professional advises otherwise. From 18 months to 6 years, use a pea-sized amount of low-fluoride children’s toothpaste. From 6 years, use a pea-sized amount of standard fluoride toothpaste. Source: Australian Dental Association.

items.question: What is the Child Dental Benefits Schedule?
items.answer: the Child Dental Benefits Schedule (CDBS) is an Australian Government program that helps eligible families with the cost of some basic dental services for children. Eligibility depends on age and on whether your family receives certain government payments, and a benefit cap applies. Check your eligibility with Services Australia, and ask reception how it works at our practice.

items.question: Does professional whitening damage teeth?
items.answer: When you use a whitening product recommended and supervised by your dental professional, whitening is considered safe and doesn’t cause permanent damage to your teeth. Some products sold online contain very high concentrations of bleaching agent that can harm teeth, which is why we don’t recommend them. Teeth whitening

items.question: Will whitening work on my fillings or crowns?
items.answer: No. Fillings and crowns don’t whiten like natural teeth, so the result can look patchy if you have them on your front teeth. Replacing them to match, or veneers, may be options. Your dentist will check before you start.

items.question: How long does Invisalign take?
items.answer: It depends on your teeth. Some minor cases take as little as 7 weeks, but around 12 to 18 months is typical. You’ll need to wear retainers afterwards to keep your result. Invisalign

items.question: How long until an implant tooth is fitted?
items.answer: The permanent tooth is usually fitted after the implant has healed and settled, typically about 3 months after it is placed. Your dentist will give you a timeline at your consultation. Dental implants

items.question: How many appointments do veneers take?
items.answer: Usually two. At the first, your teeth are prepared and impressions taken, and temporary veneers are fitted. At the second, your permanent veneers are bonded in place. Cosmetic veneers

items.question: Can I talk about a treatment before deciding?
items.answer: Yes. Your dentist will explain whether a treatment suits you, the alternatives and the likely costs. You never have to decide on the spot. Services overview

items.question: What counts as a dental emergency?
items.answer: A painful tooth or gums, broken teeth or fillings, facial swelling, trauma to your face, teeth or gums, and a broken or lost denture. Emergency dental care

items.question: Can I be seen today?
items.answer: We reserve appointments every day for dental emergencies and always try to see you as soon as possible, but we can’t guarantee a same-day time. Call as early in the day as you can.

items.question: When should I go to hospital instead?
items.answer: call 000 or go to a hospital emergency department if there is difficulty breathing or swallowing, swelling spreading to the eye or neck, bleeding that won’t stop, or a head injury. For health advice any time, Queensland’s 13 HEALTH line is on 13 43 25 84.

items.question: How much will my treatment cost?
items.answer: That depends on what your mouth needs. After your consultation, your printed treatment plan gives the most accurate estimate we can of the time and cost involved, before any treatment begins.

items.question: Do you offer payment plans?
items.answer: We can arrange interest-free payment plans through Zip for dental treatment. Ask reception about the options and terms currently available.

items.question: Can I claim on my private health insurance?
items.answer: If you have extras cover, your fund may contribute towards some treatment. What you get back depends on your policy, waiting periods and limits, so check with your fund. Bring your card to your appointment.

items.question: Is there a fee for an implant consultation?
items.answer: We offer a complimentary implant consultation to check whether implants suit you and to discuss your plan and costs. Before treatment goes ahead, a mould of your teeth and a special 3D X-ray are needed, so ask reception about any costs for these.

items.question: Does Medicare cover dental care?
items.answer: Medicare doesn’t cover most dental services. Eligible children may be covered for some basic services under the Child Dental Benefits Schedule. Some Queenslanders with concession cards may be eligible for public dental services through Queensland Health.

settings.title: Privacy policy
settings.lead: Your health information is personal. This page explains how South Cairns Dental handles it.

settings.body:
What we collect

To provide safe dental care we collect information such as your name, contact details, date of birth, medical and dental history, medicines, health fund details, and records of your treatment, including X-rays and photographs.

Why we collect it

We use your information to provide and plan your care, communicate with you about appointments, process payments and health fund claims, and meet our legal and professional obligations.

Who we share it with

We only share your information when it’s needed for your care or allowed by law. For example, we may share it with another health practitioner you’re referred to, a dental laboratory making your crown or denture, or your health fund when processing a claim. We don’t sell personal information.

How we store it

Records are kept securely, and access is limited to people who need it to do their work.

Accessing and correcting your information

You can ask to see your records or to correct information that is wrong. Contact reception on (07) 4055 4214 or reception@southcairnsdental.com.au.

This website

This website doesn’t use analytics or advertising cookies. The contact form doesn’t send or store anything itself; it opens your own email app. The map on some pages is provided by Google, which may set its own cookies under Google’s privacy policy.

Questions and complaints

If you have a concern about how we’ve handled your information, please contact us first so we can try to resolve it. If you’re not satisfied, you can contact the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.

settings.title: Check-ups and cleans
settings.lead: New patients of every age are welcome. For a first visit we recommend a thorough consultation and clean, so your dentist can see the whole picture and find small problems before they become big ones.

settings.heading: Why regular check-ups matter
settings.body:
Tooth decay and gum disease often develop without pain. By the time a tooth aches, the problem is usually larger and treatment more involved. A check-up gives your dentist the chance to spot early changes and deal with them simply.

A professional scale and clean removes calculus (hardened plaque) that a toothbrush can’t shift. Left in place, it irritates the gums and makes gum disease more likely.
settings.aside_title: Book a check-up sooner if you notice
settings.aside_items:
Gums that bleed when you brush or floss
Sensitivity to hot, cold or sweet food
A chipped tooth or a filling that feels rough
Persistent bad breath or a bad taste
A sore spot in your mouth that hasn’t healed after two weeks

settings.title: Prevention costs less, and hurts less, than repair.
settings.text: Regular check-ups let your dentist find decay, gum disease and wear early, when treatment is simpler. Ask your dentist how often you should come in; it depends on your own teeth and history.

settings.heading: What happens at your visit
settings.intro: We take sufficient time at each visit. Not every step is needed every time, and your dentist will explain what they’re doing and why.

items.title: Teeth and gums examined
items.text: A careful look at every tooth, your gums and the soft tissues of your mouth.

items.title: Jaw joints checked
items.text: Your dentist assesses how your jaw moves and whether there are signs of strain or grinding.

items.title: X-rays, if needed
items.text: Close-up and full-face X-rays show what can’t be seen by eye, such as decay between teeth or below the gum line.

items.title: Photos of anything to watch
items.text: Intraoral photos let you see exactly what your dentist sees.

items.title: Scale, clean and polish
items.text: Plaque and hardened tartar are removed and teeth are polished smooth.

items.title: Topical fluoride
items.text: Applied to help strengthen tooth enamel.

items.title: A printed treatment plan
items.text: If anything needs attention, you take home the most accurate estimate we can give of the time and cost involved.

settings.heading: Before and after your appointment
settings.intro: Always follow the instructions your dentist gives you for your own treatment.

items.title: Before your visit
items.text: Note any medicines you take and changes to your health, and any teeth that have been bothering you.

items.title: At the appointment
items.text: Tell your dentist if anything feels uncomfortable. They can pause or adjust what they’re doing.

items.title: Afterwards
items.text: Keep brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between your teeth. Your dentist will suggest when to come back.

items.question: Do I need X-rays every visit?
items.answer: No. Your dentist decides when X-rays are useful, based on your history and what they see. They show decay between teeth and problems below the gum line that can’t be seen by eye.

items.question: Will the clean hurt?
items.answer: Most people find a scale and clean comfortable. If your gums are inflamed or your teeth are sensitive, it can feel a little uncomfortable. Tell your dentist and they can go more gently.

items.answer: So you can see exactly what has been recommended and think it over in your own time. Nothing goes ahead until you’re ready.

settings.lead: A good experience early on shapes how children feel about the dentist for life. We keep visits calm, friendly and unhurried.

settings.heading: Why baby teeth matter
settings.body:
Baby teeth help children chew, speak clearly and hold space for adult teeth. Decay in baby teeth can cause pain and infection, and can affect the adult teeth developing underneath.

Regular visits let your dentist check how teeth and jaws are developing, apply preventive care where it helps, and give you practical advice for brushing and diet at each age.

White, brown or dark spots on the teeth
Your child complains of toothache or avoids chewing on one side

settings.title: Fillings
settings.lead: When decay is found early, your dentist removes the damaged part of the tooth and restores it with a white, tooth-coloured filling. It’s usually one straightforward appointment.

settings.heading: How a filling works
settings.body:
Decay is caused by bacteria that produce acid and soften the tooth. Once a cavity forms, the tooth can’t repair itself. Your dentist removes the softened, decayed part and fills the space to restore the tooth’s shape and seal it.

Fillings can also repair small chips and worn areas. The best material depends on the size and position of the filling and the forces on that tooth, and your dentist will explain the options.

settings.heading: Why it’s worth treating decay early
settings.intro: Decay doesn’t heal on its own. Left alone, it tends to move deeper into the tooth.

items.title: Early decay
items.text: Often no pain at all. Found at a check-up or on an X-ray.

items.title: A filling
items.text: Decayed material is removed and the tooth is restored with white filling material.

items.title: Deeper damage
items.text: Decay can reach the nerve, and the tooth may then need root canal therapy.

items.title: Losing the tooth
items.text: Some teeth become too damaged to save and need to be removed.

settings.heading: Benefits and things to consider
settings.intro: Your dentist will explain the benefits, risks and alternatives that apply to you.

items.title: Possible benefits
items.list:
Stops decay spreading further into the tooth
Usually completed in one appointment
Tooth-coloured material blends in with your teeth

items.title: Things to consider
items.list:
Fillings can wear, chip or need replacing over time
Large cavities may be better suited to a crown
Teeth can be sensitive for a short time afterwards

items.title: Alternatives to ask about
items.list: A crown for heavily damaged teeth Monitoring very early decay with extra prevention, where suitable

settings.heading: Before and after your appointment
settings.intro: Always follow the instructions your dentist gives you for your own treatment.

items.title: Straight after
items.text: If you’ve had local anaesthetic, avoid hot drinks and chewing until the numbness wears off, so you don’t bite your lip or cheek.

items.title: The next few days
items.text: Mild sensitivity is common and usually settles. Call us if your bite feels high or pain gets worse.

items.title: Long term
items.text: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth and keep up regular check-ups.

settings.title: Mouthguards
settings.lead: A mouthguard is worn over the upper teeth during contact sport. One made from impressions of your own teeth fits closely, stays put and is easier to talk and breathe in.

settings.heading: Custom-fitted or off the shelf?
settings.body:
Over-the-counter mouthguards come in standard sizes, or are softened in hot water and shaped by biting. A custom mouthguard is made from impressions of your own teeth, so it fits closely and is less likely to move during a hit.

A mouthguard that’s comfortable is more likely to be worn, and a well-fitted guard makes it easier to breathe, speak and drink during play.

settings.intro: No mouthguard prevents every injury, but a good one reduces the risk.

Jaw fractures
Damage to the jaw joints
Cuts to the lips and cheeks

settings.intro: Always follow the instructions your dentist gives you for your own treatment.

items.title: Keep it cool

items.title: Check it

settings.title: Crowns and bridges
settings.lead: Two ways to restore strength and appearance: a crown protects a tooth you still have, while a bridge fills the gap where a tooth is missing.

settings.heading: How crowns and bridges are made
settings.body:
For a crown, the tooth is shaped to make room, an impression or scan is taken, and a temporary crown protects the tooth while the permanent one is made. At a later appointment the permanent crown is fitted and adjusted so your bite feels right.

A bridge works in a similar way, with the teeth either side of a gap prepared to support a replacement tooth joined between them. Crowns and bridges can be made from different materials, and your dentist will explain which suits the position of the tooth.

settings.heading: Crown or bridge?
settings.intro: The right choice depends on your teeth, so it starts with an examination. Your dentist will look at the tooth, the teeth around it and your bite, then explain the options, including dental implants where they may be suitable.

items.title: Crown
items.text: A cap that covers the whole visible part of a tooth, reinforcing it.
items.list: Often considered for: a tooth that is cracked, badly decayed or has a large filling. What it does: holds the tooth together and protects it from further damage. Your own tooth: stays in place underneath the crown.

items.title: Bridge
items.text: An artificial tooth joined to the natural teeth on either side of a gap.
items.list: Often considered for: replacing one or more missing teeth. What it does: closes the gap so you can chew and smile with confidence. Neighbouring teeth: support the bridge, so their health matters.

settings.heading: Benefits and things to consider
settings.intro: Your dentist will explain the benefits, risks and alternatives that apply to you.

items.title: Possible benefits
items.list:
Protects a weakened tooth from breaking
Restores chewing and appearance
A bridge is fixed in place, so there’s nothing to remove

items.title: Things to consider
items.list:
Preparing a tooth removes some tooth structure, and this can’t be undone
Bridges rely on healthy neighbouring teeth
Crowns and bridges can need repair or replacement over time

items.title: Alternatives to ask about
items.list: A large filling in some cases A dental implant to replace a missing tooth Partial dentures

settings.heading: Looking after a crown or bridge
settings.intro: Always follow the instructions your dentist gives you for your own treatment.

items.title: With a temporary
items.text: Avoid sticky and very hard foods, and take care flossing around it.

items.title: Cleaning a bridge
items.text: Clean under the replacement tooth every day. Your dentist can show you how, using floss threaders or small brushes.

items.title: Ongoing
items.text: Regular check-ups let your dentist check the edges of the crown or bridge and the health of the teeth supporting it.

items.answer: The tooth is numbed with local anaesthetic before it’s prepared. Some sensitivity afterwards is common and usually settles.

settings.title: Root canal therapy
settings.lead: When the nerve inside a tooth is badly inflamed or has died, root canal treatment can often save the tooth rather than removing it.

settings.heading: Saving your natural tooth
settings.body:
Root canal treatment removes the inflamed or infected tissue from inside the tooth, cleans the canals and seals them. The aim is to relieve pain and infection and keep your own tooth in place.

Not every tooth can be saved, and your dentist will explain the likely outcome for yours, along with the alternatives.
settings.aside_title: Signs a tooth may need assessment
settings.aside_items:
Severe or lingering toothache
Pain that lingers after hot or cold food
Pain when biting or touching the tooth
Swelling or a pimple on the gum near a tooth

settings.title: Wisdom teeth
settings.lead: Wisdom teeth don’t always cause trouble, and they don’t always need to come out. A proper assessment tells you which situation you’re in.

settings.heading: Why wisdom teeth can cause trouble
settings.body:
Wisdom teeth are the last teeth to come through, usually in the late teens or twenties. If there isn’t enough room, they can stay partly or fully under the gum, or come through at an angle. This is often called an impacted wisdom tooth.

A partly erupted tooth can trap food and bacteria, leading to inflamed gums and infection. Many wisdom teeth cause no problems at all, which is why assessment comes before any decision.

settings.title: Swelling that spreads?
settings.text: Swelling that spreads to your eye or neck, or makes it hard to swallow or breathe, needs urgent medical attention. Call 000 or see our emergency page.

settings.title: Dental implants
settings.lead: An implant replaces the root of a missing tooth and supports a new tooth on top. It’s fixed in place, so there’s nothing to take out at night.

settings.heading: How an implant replaces a tooth
settings.body:
A dental implant has three parts: a post placed in the jawbone that acts as the root, a connector called an abutment, and a crown that looks like a natural tooth. Over the healing period, the bone bonds to the implant, giving it a strong foundation.

Implants can replace a single tooth, several teeth, or support a bridge or denture.

settings.lead: Professional whitening is a safe and effective way to brighten your smile. A specially designed whitening gel lifts discolouration that has built up over time.

settings.heading: What whitening can and can’t do
settings.body:
Professional whitening uses a bleaching gel to lighten the natural colour of tooth enamel. Results vary from person to person, depending on the cause of discolouration and your natural tooth shade.

Whitening doesn’t change the colour of fillings, crowns or veneers, and some types of staining respond better than others. Your dentist will check your teeth first and give you realistic expectations.

items.question: Does whitening damage your teeth?
items.answer: When you use a whitening product recommended and supervised by your dental professional, whitening is considered safe and doesn’t cause permanent damage to your teeth. Some systems sold online contain very high concentrations of bleaching agent that can damage teeth, and your dentist won’t recommend those. Your dentist also checks your teeth and gums first, so problems like decay or gum disease are dealt with before you start.

items.question: Will my teeth be sensitive?
items.answer: Some patients notice mild sensitivity during whitening. It is temporary and returns to your normal level once you stop. If whitening trays are overfilled, the gums can briefly feel a slight burning and look white; this also settles quickly once the gel is rinsed away. Tell your dentist if your teeth are already sensitive.

items.question: How often will I need to whiten?
items.answer: It varies from person to person, and depends a lot on diet and lifestyle. If you drink a lot of tea, coffee or red wine, or smoke, you’ll generally need to whiten more often. On average, a touch-up may be needed about every 6 months. Your dentist can suggest a schedule for you.

items.question: I have fillings or crowns on my front teeth. Can I still whiten?
items.answer: Whitening works on natural tooth enamel. It doesn’t change the colour of fillings, crowns or veneers. Your dentist will discuss how this affects your result, and whether those restorations may need updating afterwards to match. Sometimes veneers are a better option.

To fit a veneer, a thin layer of enamel is usually removed from the front of the tooth so the veneer sits naturally. This step is permanent, so veneers are a long-term commitment.

settings.title: Invisalign
settings.lead: Invisalign uses a series of clear, removable trays. Each set moves your teeth a little, until they reach their planned position.

settings.heading: How clear aligner treatment works
settings.body:
After an assessment, your dentist takes scans or impressions and plans the movement of your teeth. A series of custom aligners is made, and you change to the next set as directed. You’ll have regular reviews to check progress.

Aligners only work while they’re in your mouth. They need to be worn for most of the day and night, taken out only to eat, drink anything other than water, and clean your teeth.

items.title: Discreet
items.text: The trays are clear, so most people won’t notice them.

items.title: Removable
items.text: Take them out to eat, brush and floss.

items.title: No metal
items.text: No brackets or wires to rub your cheeks and gums.

items.title: Suitability is assessed first
items.text: A trained dentist checks whether aligners can achieve what you need. Some people are better suited to braces or an orthodontist, and we’ll tell you if that’s the case.

items.title: Records and your trays
items.text: X-rays, photos and moulds of your teeth are taken, and you usually start in your trays within a few weeks.

items.title: Often 12 to 18 months
items.text: Some minor cases take as little as 7 weeks, but around 12 to 18 months is typical. Your plan will give you an estimate.

items.title: Retainers afterwards
items.text: Teeth tend to drift back, so you’ll need a retainer to hold the result.

settings.title: Emergency dental care
settings.lead: We reserve appointments every day for dental emergencies. Call as early in the day as you can, tell us what’s happened, and we’ll do our best to fit you in. Please call rather than walking in.

settings.heading: Don’t wait with a dental emergency
settings.body:
Dental emergencies can be painful and distressing, and if left untreated they can get worse quickly. That’s why we reserve specific appointments every day for them. If you have a dental emergency, call us straight away. We’ll always try to see you as soon as possible.

You don’t need to be an existing patient, and we see children and adults.
settings.aside_items:
A painful tooth or gums
Broken teeth or fillings
Facial swelling
Trauma to your face, teeth or gums
A broken or lost denture

settings.title: Call 000 or go to your nearest hospital emergency department
settings.text: If there is difficulty breathing or swallowing, swelling spreading to the eye or neck, heavy bleeding that won’t stop, or a head injury such as loss of consciousness. Don’t wait for a dental appointment.

settings.heading: First aid while you wait
settings.intro: Simple steps that may help until you can see us. Your dentist’s advice always comes first.

items.title: Painful teeth or gums
items.text: Toothache, throbbing, or pain when biting or with hot and cold.
items.list:
Rinse gently with warm water.
Floss carefully in case food is trapped.
Pain relief from your pharmacy may help. Follow the label and check with your pharmacist that it suits you.
Don’t put tablets directly on your gum.

items.title: Broken teeth or fillings
items.text: A chipped, cracked or broken tooth, or a filling that has fallen out.
items.list:
Keep any broken pieces and bring them with you.
Rinse gently with warm water.
Chew on the other side and avoid very hot, cold or hard food.

items.title: Facial swelling
items.text: Swelling of the gum, cheek or jaw, which can be a sign of infection.
items.list:
Call us promptly. Swelling shouldn’t be left to see if it settles.
A cold compress on the outside of the cheek may ease discomfort.
items.flag: If swelling affects your breathing, swallowing or eye, or you feel very unwell with a fever, call 000 or go to hospital.

items.title: A knocked-out adult tooth
items.text: A knock from sport, a fall or an accident.
items.list:
Act quickly. Pick it up by the crown (the white part), not the root.
If it’s dirty, rinse it briefly in milk or water. Don’t scrub it.
If you can, gently put it back in its socket and bite on a clean cloth. Otherwise keep it in milk.
Call us straight away.
items.flag: Don’t try to put a baby tooth back in. Call us for advice. Any head injury needs medical assessment first.

items.title: Broken or lost dentures
items.text: Dentures that have cracked, snapped or been lost.
items.list:
Don’t glue or repair them yourself.
Keep all the pieces and bring them with you.
If a sharp edge is rubbing, leave the denture out.

items.title: Not sure if it’s urgent?
items.text: If something doesn’t feel right, call and describe it. Reception can help you work out how soon you need to be seen.

settings.heading: What happens when you call
settings.intro: Have a pen handy. Reception may give you a time and some instructions.

items.title: Tell us what’s happened
items.text: When it started, where it hurts, and whether there’s swelling, bleeding or a broken tooth.

items.title: We look for the soonest time
items.text: We reserve emergency appointments each day and will try to see you as soon as we can.

items.title: Your dentist relieves the problem
items.text: The first goal is to treat pain or infection. If more treatment is needed, your dentist will explain the options for a later visit.

items.title: After hours and weekends
items.text: After-hours and weekend appointments are available on request. Ask reception when you call during opening hours: Mon to Thu 8 am to 5 pm, Fri 8 am to 4:30 pm.

items.title: Health advice any time
items.text: Queensland’s 13 HEALTH line is on 13 43 25 84, 24 hours a day.

items.title: Life-threatening
items.text: Call 000.

items.question: Can you guarantee to see me today?
items.answer: We can’t promise a same-day appointment, but we keep time free every day for emergencies and will do everything we can. Calling early in the day gives you the best chance.

items.question: Do you see children for emergencies?
items.answer: Yes. We treat children and adults. Call us and tell reception your child’s age and what has happened.

items.question: I’m not a patient yet. Can I still call?
items.answer: Yes. You don’t need to be an existing patient to call us about a dental emergency.

posts.title: Why choose dental implants?
posts.excerpt: Dental implants are a proven way to replace one or more missing teeth. Here are the main advantages, and how to find out whether an implant suits you.
posts.content:
Dental implants are a simple and proven method to replace one or more missing teeth. A titanium post is placed in the jawbone, and a tooth (crown) is then fixed on top.

What are the advantages of dental implants?

  • Fully fixed in place, so it can’t fall out like a denture
  • Looks like a natural tooth
  • Functions and chews like a natural tooth
  • Helps stop neighbouring teeth drifting into the gap
  • Helps prevent the jawbone shrinking away where the tooth was removed

Is an implant right for me?

Implants aren’t the right choice for everyone, and they’re not the only way to replace a tooth. A bridge or a denture may suit you better. At a consultation your dentist will look at your teeth, gums and jawbone, explain the options and talk you through the costs before anything goes ahead. Read more about dental implants.
